WHO.title: Doing what matters in times of stress: An illustrated guide

tips.text: Take two minutes to notice your body: hungry, thirsty, needing the bathroom, too hot or cold, or in pain? Take care of the easiest one first.
Drink some water and have a small snack if it’s been a while. Running low can make your thinking foggy and your mood worse.
Take a 5–10 minute break that asks nothing of you. If you nap, about 20 minutes keeps it from messing with night sleep.
Cross off or postpone one thing today. Realistic goals protect your energy.
Try to wake up around the same time every day, weekends too, within about an hour.
Give yourself some quiet, screen-free time before bed if that works for you. (If a show or audio calms you, that’s okay too.)
Make your bedroom quiet, cool, and dark. A dim night light is fine.
Have your last caffeine earlier in the day, since it can last up to 8 hours, and skip alcohol and big meals close to bedtime.
Get a few minutes of daylight during the day if you can.
Keep a water bottle where you’ll see it, or set a reminder. Thirst signals can be easy to miss.
If you haven’t eaten in a while, any food counts. Start with something easy you like.
Keep a few easy, low-effort foods you like on hand for low-energy days.
Have water with meals. Chilling it or adding lemon can make it easier.
A 5–10 minute walk counts, even indoors. Short bits of movement add up.
Stand up and stretch between long stretches of sitting.
Pick movement you actually like, such as dancing, gardening, or chair exercises.
If you have a health condition or disability, do what your body allows today, and ask your clinician what suits you. Rest counts.
Send one low-pressure message to someone you trust, like a meme or a “thinking of you.”
Low-demand time together counts: texting, a video call, or just being in the same room doing your own things.
Do one small kind thing for someone, like a thank-you or really listening.
Look for a community or support group where you can be yourself without masking.
Spend 10 minutes on a hobby or special interest, just because you like it.
Write down one to three specific things you’re grateful for today.
Try one tiny new thing: a recipe, a song, a craft.
Name one thing that matters to you and take one small step toward it.
Slow your breathing for a minute or two. If focusing on your breath feels bad, try the next idea instead.
Ground yourself: press your feet into the floor and name a few things you can see and hear.
Take a break from the news and social media.
Write down what’s on your mind for five minutes.
Notice a stressful thought, name it (“I’m having the thought that…”), and come back to what you’re doing.
Move gently or take a short walk. Activity can lift your mood a little.
Tell one person you trust how you’re really doing.
Talk to yourself the way you’d talk to a friend, and make room for the feeling instead of fighting it.
Do one small, doable thing, like a shower, a dish, or a reply, and count it as a win.
Use headphones, earplugs, or sunglasses to turn the world down.
Go somewhere quieter and dimmer for a few minutes, or lower the lights and noise where you are.
Use comfort items or stim freely: fidgets, a weighted blanket, rocking.
Plan recovery time after busy or loud events, and check ahead what a place will be like.
It’s okay to tell people you need quiet and talk less for a while.

getHelp.text: If, for two weeks or more, you have trouble sleeping, changes in appetite, trouble getting out of bed, trouble concentrating, or lose interest in things you used to enjoy, it’s a good time to talk with a doctor or therapist. A primary care provider is a good place to start.
For help finding mental health or substance use treatment, the SAMHSA National Helpline is free, confidential, and open 24/7 at 1-800-662-4357. It’s for information and referrals, not crisis support.
Exhaustion, losing skills you usually have, and lower tolerance for sensory input lasting months can be autistic burnout. Autistic adults describe needing support and accommodations, not just rest.
